messages:
serena: Quick question — I'm chasing a perf regression in KV cache handoffs. Planning an nsight capture but want to keep the trace small. Best minimal flags to reliably see kernel selection + batching handoff hotspots?

akshay: For KV handoffs I usually do a targeted nvtx-bracketed capture. Short pattern: warm up, start NVTX marker, run a few real requests, stop. Use -t cuda,nvtx,osrt to get kernel, nvtx markers and OS runtime events.

leo: +1. Example we use:```
nsys profile -o kv-handoff-run -t cuda,nvtx,osrt --sample=cpu --force-overwrite --capture-range=nvtx --capture-range-start=nvtx:KV_START --capture-range-end=nvtx:KV_END -- python -u tests/infer_kv_handoff.py
```

serena: Nice. How long do you set the capture window? I'm worried about file size and sampling noise.

akshay: Keep it short — capture only when NVTX markers are active. If you can't bracket, then 10-30s is fine for a few iterations: big win is avoiding full-training traces. Sampling (cpu) gives you stack samples in hotspots without huge telemetry; if you need full CUDA API timeline remove --sample to get exact kernel launches but larger files.

leo: Also toggle the OSRT trace so you can correlate pthreads/syscalls with kernel spikes. Without osrt it's harder to see GC/warmup pauses that shift kernel selection.

serena: Any tips for kv-cache warmup vs steady-state? The regression appears after a few requests.

akshay: Warmup first outside capture for ~50 requests so caches/KV states are stable. Then start nvtx bracket and reproduce the slow requests. Also include nvtx markers around batching boundary: KV_PREFETCH_START, BATCH_DISPATCH_START, KERNEL_COMPLETE — that makes the timeline trivially searchable.

leo: If you see intermittent long gaps between cuLaunchKernels check for host-side stalls: look at OSRT thread wakeups and CPU sampling stacks (pthread_cond_wait / epoll). Those often indicate batching heuristic flip/flop (e.g., batch grouping drops from 8->1).

serena: Example of a short grep I ran on the nsys report:```
# quick pyflame-like sample counts
nsys stats kv-handoff-run.qdrep | grep "cuLaunchKernel" -A2
```

perf-bot: FYI: file size tip — add `-x true` (enable file compression) and `--output=kv-handoff-run` so you only keep the .qdrep/.nsys-rep you need. Also `--stop-after` can stop after the child process exits.

akshay: One more thing: if kernel selection seems to switch by sequence length, capture different sequence length buckets separately. Run short, medium, long sequences in separate bracketed captures. Kernel timelines will often show two different kernel names (fast_int8_kernel_vX vs dense_fp16_kernel_vY).

leo: When you get the qdrep open it in Nsight UI and use the ‘Kernel Details’ + ‘API Trace’ lanes. Look for a pattern: repeated small kernels (prefetch / kv_unpack) preceding a heavy matmul. If the small kernels saturate the stream they can change scheduling/qualify for a different kernel launch path.

serena: This is great — I'll run a warmup, bracket, 20s NVTX capture with cpu sampling + osrt and send the qdrep. Will add explicit NVTX markers for KV_PREFETCH/BATCH_DISPATCH/KERNEL_DONE.

akshay: If you need, tag me in the thread and attach the qdrep + `nsys stats --report=overview kv-handoff-run.qdrep` output. We can triage kernel timelines and look for candidate kernels to force-quantize/replace. :mag:

leo: And remember to check the kernel SM utilization and active warps; low occupancy on the big matmul often points to the wrong kernel variant being picked by our runtime selection heuristics.

serena: Will do. Thanks both! :rocket:
